items.title: Show HN: Fraise: a memory database for AI agents
items.summary:
Fraise is a memory database for AI agents — a single binary that stores facts as a temporal graph of facts, topics and entities, queried in a small language with
two verbs: ```
  remember 'acme moved to annual billing' topic:billing entity:acme
  recall billing entity:acme since:30d top:5
``` Two verbs because the caller pays for every token it reads back. A recall is ranked and capped rather than exhaustive, with recent facts outranking older ones. Unlike most memory layers that use existing databases (vector, graph) to index data, Fraise provides a lightweight, no infrastructure layer that is designed to be used directly by agents: hence the simple query language to manage memory. Fraise has a hybrid (graph, text and vector) retrieval engine: text and vector are used to find seeds, which are starting points for the graph search. The Fraise graph is bipartite: facts linked to entities and / or topics. It ships an MCP server (that I actually use now with my Claude Code sessions). Which means that memory persists across sessions. 
You can use `claude mcp add fraise -- fraise mcp` to set it up. It also supports Codex (all instructions available in the docs). I benchmarked it against mem0, Letta, Graphiti, EverOS and cognee on LoCoMo, with every system ingesting the same conversations using the same extraction model and the same embedding model, and answering the same questions. Retrieval recall at k=10: 0.893 against a best of 0.897, at 0.18s p50 (twice as fast as the next system) and about a third of the tokens of the highest scorer. Scalability-wise, writes are essentially linear, but reads grow linearly with vertex degree (e.g. a topic with 30K facts attached costs about 55× than one with 500). This is 0.1.0 so plenty of work to do. As mentioned above, scalability with adversarial graph topologies, but also persistency: for now Fraise is in memory with no file storage. This is the first feature for 0.2.0. If this is a topic that is of interest, I'd love to chat, or if you have any feedback feel free to reach out! Repo: https://github.com/FraiseHQ/fraise Docs: https://docs.getfraise.dev Comments URL: https://news.ycombinator.com/item?id=49609014 Points: 1 # Comments: 0

Fraise is a memory database for AI agents — a single binary that stores facts as a temporal graph of facts, topics and entities, queried in a small language with two verbs:

``` remember 'acme moved to annual billing' topic:billing entity:acme recall billing entity:acme since:30d top:5 ```

Two verbs because the caller pays for every token it reads back. A recall is ranked and capped rather than exhaustive, with recent facts outranking older ones.

Unlike most memory layers that use existing databases (vector, graph) to index data, Fraise provides a lightweight, no infrastructure layer that is designed to be used directly by agents: hence the simple query language to manage memory.

Fraise has a hybrid (graph, text and vector) retrieval engine: text and vector are used to find seeds, which are starting points for the graph search. The Fraise graph is bipartite: facts linked to entities and / or topics.

It ships an MCP server (that I actually use now with my Claude Code sessions). Which means that memory persists across sessions. You can use `claude mcp add fraise -- fraise mcp` to set it up. It also supports Codex (all instructions available in the docs).

I benchmarked it against mem0, Letta, Graphiti, EverOS and cognee on LoCoMo, with every system ingesting the same conversations using the same extraction model and the same embedding model, and answering the same questions. Retrieval recall at k=10: 0.893 against a best of 0.897, at 0.18s p50 (twice as fast as the next system) and about a third of the tokens of the highest scorer. Scalability-wise, writes are essentially linear, but reads grow linearly with vertex degree (e.g. a topic with 30K facts attached costs about 55× than one with 500).

This is 0.1.0 so plenty of work to do. As mentioned above, scalability with adversarial graph topologies, but also persistency: for now Fraise is in memory with no file storage. This is the first feature for 0.2.0.

If this is a topic that is of interest, I'd love to chat, or if you have any feedback feel free to reach out!

items.title: My dream is to become a chairman who only gave KPIs for AI, not tasks
items.summary:
My dream is to become a chairman who focuses on investing then the company figures out how to make money. When AI agents raising, I also tried vibe coding for building products, but I feel tired when still being in loop with them for building and testing. Then I came across with idea for a company operated by agents based on KPIs, not tasks. The only one thing I need to do is gave KPIs to CEO (smartest agent), then It break down as a list to Managers and Managers delivery it to team member. Or If I don't give any KPIs, Managers will daily and report to CEO what changes, what nexts to do, then CEO report to me. Human Chairman
       |
     AI CEO
   /    |     \
Product Growth Engineering
   |      |       |
specialists   Developer/DevOps I was using it for some KPIs with my website twitee.co (an alternative Xcancel, Nitter, Twitterwebviewer)
- Increase traffic 10% every week.
- Do market research what user needs then turn it to product features.
- Deploy and monitor system, improve infra if needs. --- The real story unexpected is I did set up k3s in macmini for hosting website, it was good, but when Xcancel, Nitter received cease and desist notices and shutdown, the traffic increased unnormal and macmini down at midnight, next day from CEO report, it said that there is a chance and it asked me a budget to scale up, but I actually not aware of it. I am not claiming that the agents can autonomously run but this model was very interesting. I feel free without stress. It is still an experiment, share for anyone who also tired with vibe coding, you can try it here: 
https://github.com/nohuman-labs/agent-company Comments URL: https://news.ycombinator.com/item?id=49608984 Points: 1 # Comments: 0
